mcqs.question: Running the same declarative IaC config a second time, with no changes to it or the environment, typically results in what?
options: No changes — the tool diffs desired vs actual state and finds nothing to do
A duplicate set of resources being created
An error, since the resources already exist
The resources are deleted and recreated from scratch
mcqs.explanation: Declarative tools compare desired state (the code) against actual state and only act on the difference — with no difference, a re-run is a safe no-op. Duplicating resources or erroring on re-run is the signature of imperative, non-idempotent scripting, not declarative IaC.

mcqs.question: Which property must an IaC pipeline have to safely apply the same config on every merge to main, without manual checks each time?
mcqs.explanation: Idempotency — the same run producing the same result whether applied once or many times — is exactly what makes it safe to automate apply on every merge. Statelessness, immutability, and concurrency are related infrastructure concepts but don't describe this specific 'safe to rerun' guarantee.

mcqs.question: A team version-controls a bash script that calls `aws-cli create-*` commands in sequence. Why doesn't this provide the same guarantees as real IaC?
options: Bash scripts can't be stored in git
AWS CLI commands are inherently less secure than Terraform
It lacks a diff/plan step and isn't idempotent by default — rerunning it can fail or duplicate resources
It actually does provide the same guarantees — version control is the only thing that matters
mcqs.explanation: The defining gap is behavioral, not about where the code lives: a script full of imperative create-calls has no built-in state tracking or plan step, so it can't safely tell you what will change before it happens, and reruns often error or duplicate resources. Version control alone doesn't grant idempotency or a plan/diff capability.

mcqs.question: A team provisions a VM with Terraform, then uses Ansible to install packages and configure users on it. Is this a redundant use of two IaC tools?
options: No -- Terraform answers what infrastructure resources should exist, while Ansible answers what should be configured on a running machine; they compose rather than compete
Yes -- either tool alone can fully replace the other for any use case
No, but only because Ansible is required to run before Terraform
Yes -- configuration management tools are obsolete now that IaC tools exist
mcqs.explanation: IaC and configuration management solve different problems -- provisioning resources vs. configuring what runs on them -- so pairing them is a standard pattern, not redundancy. There's no required ordering that Ansible must precede Terraform, and neither tool makes the other obsolete.
